question:
Patient note:
A 35-year-old man with no documented medical conditions and no prescription medications was air-lifted from a commercial construction site after co-workers witnessed him topple backward off the second-story decking and land supine on packed dirt; they report a brief gasp followed by silence, with neither limb convulsions nor vomitus observed, and they applied no first aid beyond maintaining cervical alignment with their hands until paramedics arrived nine minutes later. Flight crew placed a rigid collar, log-rolled him onto a vacuum mattress, inserted a single 18-gauge catheter into the right antecubital vein that was flushed only with 5 mL saline, and delivered 4 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula because respirations were spontaneous but shallow; they administered no crystalloids, opioids, benzodiazepines, paralytics, antiemetics, dextrose, or vasoactive agents during the seventeen-minute transport. On touchdown he was transferred directly to the trauma bay still secured in full spinal precautions, clothing caked with red clay but free of blood beyond a 2-cm oozing laceration behind the left auricle. Initial pre-intervention vitals obtained concurrently with the first head-to-toe assessment showed blood pressure 138/82 mm Hg in the left brachial artery, heart rate 94 beats/min in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min with symmetrical chest excursion, oxygen saturation 95 % on the same nasal cannula, and core temperature 37.0 °C via esophageal probe placed by flight crew. Airway exam revealed intact dentition, a midline tongue, and copious gravel dust lining the gingiva yet no pooled secretions; a Yankauer tip touching the soft palate provoked a robust gag and two-second cough. Breath sounds were vesicular and equal, percussion resonant, and there was no accessory muscle use. Cardiac auscultation produced a crisp S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; radial and dorsalis pedis pulses were 2+ bilaterally and capillary refill was under two seconds. Abdomen was flat, soft, and non-tender; pelvis was stable to gentle compression. Long-bone survey identified mild swelling over the right forearm without crepitus or deformity; distal pulses and motor function in all extremities were present. During a silent forty-second observation the patient lay motionless with eyelids fully shut; lashes did not flutter and there was no spontaneous ocular movement. Repeated calling of his first name at conversational and then shout-level volume failed to elicit any reaction. When a firm supra-orbital notch pressure was applied for five seconds, both lids suddenly parted to mid-palpebral height and pupils, measuring 4 mm, rotated toward the examiner before drifting superiorly once the stimulus stopped, after which the lids slowly closed again. A similar response occurred with trapezius squeeze but not in the absence of noxious input. Speech was absent at rest; however, upon nail-bed compression of the left index finger the patient blurted clearly articulated but disconnected phrases—“blue ladder… lunchtime… where’s the drill”—that bore no relevance to questions about his name, location, or the event, and he ceased phonating immediately after the pain stopped. Cranial nerve testing was otherwise notable for brisk corneal reflexes, midline uvula, and symmetric facial grimace when the mandibular condyle was pressed. Muscle tone at rest was normal. When the same nail-bed stimulus was applied to the right thumb, the contralateral (left) hand lifted off the mattress, swept across midline, and purposefully attempted to grasp and push away the examiner’s fingers; the movement was accurate and terminated once the hand made contact, after which the limb settled back to the stretcher without abnormal posturing. An identical directed reach occurred toward a trapezius pinch on either side. Lower extremities displayed only mild hip flexion but no extension or withdrawal during these tests. Deep tendon reflexes were 2+ at biceps and patellae, 1+ at Achilles; plantar stimulation produced flexor responses bilaterally. No clonus was present. Skin examination revealed scattered superficial abrasions over both scapulae and a 3 × 4 cm contusion on the right occiput without palpable step-off. Portable anterior-posterior chest and pelvic radiographs completed within five minutes were unremarkable, and a focused assessment with sonography for trauma was negative for free fluid. Point-of-care venous blood gas prior to any medication administration showed pH 7.38, pCO₂ 38 mm Hg, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L; finger-stick glucose measured 108 mg/dL. No intravenous fluids, sedatives, analgesics, hyperosmolar therapy, or paralytics have been given since arrival, ensuring that the ocular, verbal, and motor behaviors detailed above reflect his untreated neurologic baseline. Neurosurgery, orthopedic trauma, and critical care teams have been paged, and stat non-contrast head and cervical spine CT along with CT angiography of the cervical vessels are being arranged while continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and fifteen-minute neurologic checks proceed at bedside.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow Coma Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow Coma Scale sums the best eye (1–4), verbal (1–5), and motor (1–6) responses on the initial examination.
- Eye opening: his eyes remain closed spontaneously and to voice but open with supraorbital pressure. Opening to pressure = E2.
- Verbal response: he produces recognizable but unrelated words, not a conversation. Inappropriate words = V3.
- Motor response: he reaches across the midline to push the examiner's fingers away rather than simply withdrawing. Localizing the stimulus = M5.
Total = E2 + V3 + M5 = 10.
Final answer: 10
